classifications.label: Instrumental crosstalk or shared systematic error with inverted phase coupling
Weak periodic environmental oscillation (settlement-scale cycle) with 4–7 day period
Data processing or record-keeping artifact (offset misalignment, timestamp drift, or partial data duplication)

Pendulum instruments experienced a genuine environmental or instrumental step-change around day 10–12; resonators did not. The negative cross-correlations are a separate systematic artifact (crosstalk or shared inverted-phase error) affecting all four streams.

A settlement-scale periodic environmental oscillation (4–7 day cycle: thermal, hydraulic, seismic, or structural) is real. Pendulums and resonators respond inversely to this driver. The day-12 pendulum shift is a separate phenomenon or a coincidental inflection in the oscillation's envelope.

Data logging or timestamp artifact: readings are misaligned in time across instrument streams, creating spurious negative correlations at fixed offsets. The day-12 pendulum shift is real, but the cross-instrument offsets are artifacts of clock drift, record-file merging errors, or day-of-week indexing bugs.

Instrumental crosstalk or shared electromagnetic/mechanical coupling, specifically: all four instruments couple to a single noisy shared source (e.g., settlement vibration, EM interference) with *inverted* phase relationships to different instrument types. Pendulums and resonators respond oppositely because of their different mechanical/electrical sensitivities.

The day-12 pendulum shift and the negative cross-correlations are both artifacts of my own calibration or data-processing routine. I may have inadvertently introduced a systematic error when I reprocessed or re-baselined the data after day 10.

Genuine bifurcated response: pendulum instruments experienced a real environmental or instrumental step-change around day 10–12; resonators did not. Negative cross-correlations arise from a separate systematic artifact (electromagnetic crosstalk with inverted phase, or shared calibration error) affecting all four streams independently.

Settlement-scale environmental oscillation (4–7 day cycle) drives inverse responses in pendulum vs. resonator instruments. The day-12 pendulum shift is either a separate phenomenon or an inflection in the oscillation's envelope that has not reverted.

Data logging or timestamp artifact: readings are misaligned across instrument streams by consistent offsets (4–7 days), creating spurious negative correlations. The day-12 pendulum shift is real, but the cross-instrument patterns are artifacts of clock drift, record merging errors, or timestamp indexing bugs.

Instrumental crosstalk or shared electromagnetic/mechanical coupling: all four instruments couple to a single noisy source (e.g., settlement vibration, EM interference, power distribution noise) with inverted phase relationships to different instrument types. Pendulums and resonators respond oppositely because they have different mechanical/electrical sensitivities.

Self-generated data processing artifact: I inadvertently reprocessed or recalibrated pendulum data between day 10 and day 13, introducing a step-change. I did not apply the same correction to resonators, creating spurious negative correlations when post-correction pendulum data are correlated with unchanged resonator data.

Genuine bifurcated physical response: pendulums experience a step-change around day 12; resonators a separate step-change around day 16. Both reflect real environmental or instrumental events (thermal, mechanical, or gravitational) with opposite phase sensitivities. Negative cross-correlations are a secondary artifact (EM crosstalk, logging error, or shared calibration drift).

Single settlement-scale environmental oscillation (4–7 day period) with inverted phase sensitivities in pendulums vs. resonators; the day-12 pendulum inflection is the beginning of a multi-day envelope change (amplitude or mean shift) in this oscillation that does not fully revert.

Data handling artifact: readings are systematically misaligned in time across instrument streams (clock drift, day-of-week vs. absolute timestamp indexing, or record merging error), creating spurious negative correlations at fixed lags. The day-12 and day-16 level shifts are real but unrelated to the cross-correlation structure.

I introduced a data processing or calibration error between day 10 and day 13 in the pendulum stream (and possibly others), changing the conversion factors or drift-correction coefficients without recording it, and then correlated the modified stream with unmodified resonator data, producing spurious negative correlations at variable lags due to phase inversion in the error.

Instrumental crosstalk or shared mechanical/electromagnetic coupling to settlement vibration, power distribution noise, or hydraulic oscillations, with inverted phase relationships to pendulums vs. resonators. The day-12 and day-16 level shifts represent sudden changes in the strength or phase of this crosstalk (e.g., a power line reconfiguration, pump activation, or instrument re-seating).

Two independent real instrumental or environmental step-changes with opposite phase sensitivities: pendulums experience a compressive/thermal event ~day 12 that increases frequency; resonators experience a separate event ~day 16 that decreases Q or frequency. Negative cross-correlations reflect inverted mechanical responses to a shared 4–7 day environmental oscillation (thermal cycling, seismic, or human activity rhythm) that persists before, during, and after both shifts.

Data misalignment or timestamp indexing error introduced before day 12: clock skew, day-of-week vs. absolute date indexing, or record merging created spurious offsets that propagate through all cross-correlations. The level shifts are real but separate from the correlation structure.

I introduced an undocumented data processing change (gain, drift correction, or conversion factor) between day 10 and day 13, creating a step-change in one or more processed streams and spurious phase-inverted correlations when compared to unmodified streams.

Instrumental crosstalk or coupling to settlement vibration, EM noise, or hydraulic oscillations with inverted phase relationships. The day-12 and day-16 shifts represent sudden changes in crosstalk strength or phase (e.g., power distribution reconfiguration, pump activation, or accidental instrument re-seating).

Undetected systematic drift in one of the four measurement channels (or in my calibration coefficients) that began around day 11–12 for pendulums and day 15–16 for resonators, changing the baseline without my knowledge. The negative correlations are a secondary artifact of comparing a drifted channel to stable channels.

Residual: an unconsidered explanation (e.g., a non-linear interaction between instruments, an undocumented settlement event that was not in my log, a third shared physical variable I have not measured, or a statistical artifact in my correlation calculation itself).
